reasoning: Patient is unresponsive — cannot be aroused or communicates only reflex responses
Unresponsiveness alone meets ESI-1 criteria: requires immediate assessment and intervention capability
High-risk ingestion scenario: multiple alcohol bottles + unidentified empty pill bottles present at bedside
History of suicidality + unresponsive state = likely intentional overdose until proven otherwise
Vitals NOT recorded at triage — unable to assess airway patency, breathing adequacy, or perfusion status; unresponsive patients can decompensate rapidly
Age 17 (adolescent): altered mental status from any cause (toxin, hypoglycemia, head injury, status epilepticus, shock) is high-risk; pediatric patients can compensate well until sudden collapse
No prior medical record available — cannot rule out underlying seizure disorder, metabolic disease, or cardiac arrhythmia as alternative etiology
Differential includes: acute overdose, altered mental status from toxic ingestion, aspiration risk, respiratory depression, hypoglycemia, intracranial pathology
Immediate needs: continuous pulse oximetry/cardiac monitoring, IV access, rapid glucose check, airway assessment, toxicology screen, head CT consideration, possible intubation for airway protection
red_flags: Unresponsiveness — altered mental status of unknown etiology
Suicidal history + unresponsiveness + bottles of alcohol + empty pill bottles = presumed overdose
Vitals not yet obtained — cannot assess oxygenation, ventilation, or hemodynamic stability
Risk of aspiration and respiratory depression in unresponsive patient
Unknown ingestion substances and timing — cannot predict toxidrome or trajectory
Adolescent with altered mental status — broad differential; requires urgent intervention capability at bedside
No baseline medical history — cannot distinguish acute vs. chronic process
